# Template package set — what every container built from this template needs.
# Read by install-packages.sh before packages.txt.
#
# DO NOT EDIT THIS FILE TO GIVE ONE PROJECT A PACKAGE.
# That is what .devcontainer/packages.txt is for. This file is boilerplate: it
# is overwritten by /project-bootstrap --update-devcontainer, and an edit here
# is lost at that point.
#
# Format: `installer:package`, one per line, `#` for comments.
#   apt:NAME    system package        npm:NAME    global npm package
#   pip:NAME    Python package
#
# Entries here are FAIL-CLOSED: a failure aborts the container create. That is
# right for this list because it is the firewall's own tooling — a container
# that cannot raise its egress policy has not usefully been built. Project
# entries are best-effort by contrast; see packages.txt.

# --- Firewall tooling ------------------------------------------------------
# What init-firewall.sh needs to program iptables/ipset and resolve the
# allow-list. curl and iproute2 are already on the base image and are listed
# anyway, so the requirement is stated rather than inherited.
apt:iptables
apt:ipset
apt:dnsutils
apt:aggregate
apt:jq
apt:curl
apt:ca-certificates
apt:iproute2

# --- Secrets tooling -------------------------------------------------------
# age is the encryption backend sops uses, and `age-keygen` is what makes the
# key that ~/.config/sops is bound for (see mounts in devcontainer.json). It is
# in the Ubuntu archives, so it is one line here rather than another pinned
# download; Ubuntu keeps it patched, which a pin would not.
#
# sops itself is NOT here and cannot be: it is in no Ubuntu release. It is
# installed by .devcontainer/install-sops.sh from a pinned GitHub release with a
# verified SHA-256 per architecture, exactly like herdr below.
apt:age

# --- Shell niceties --------------------------------------------------------
# neofetch prints the OS / kernel / CPU / memory summary beside an ASCII logo.
#
# It is here in place of fastfetch, which is what was actually asked for.
# fastfetch is in no Ubuntu LTS archive - Launchpad has it from 25.04 (plucky)
# onward, and the base image's moving :ubuntu tag is the LTS - so shipping it
# would have meant a fourth pinned GitHub-release binary with a SHA-256 per
# architecture and its own check.sh assertions, for a system-info banner. Do
# NOT change this line to `apt:fastfetch` before that tag reaches an LTS that
# carries it: in a fail-closed list, a package that does not exist aborts every
# create.
#
# Two caveats. Upstream neofetch was archived in April 2024 and noble packages
# a 2021 release; it runs, it will not gain features, and `inxi` is the
# maintained alternative in the same archive if detail matters more than the
# logo. And a cosmetic tool in a fail-closed list can in principle cost a
# create - accepted here because it is in noble's universe component for the
# life of the LTS, and it joins the same apt transaction as the firewall
# tooling above, which already requires the Ubuntu archives to be reachable.
apt:neofetch

# Deliberately NOT here: opencode, herdr, graphify and sops.
#
# All four are installed by postCreateCommand instead, and all four should stay
# there. opencode is pinned to an exact npm version, graphify to an exact PyPI
# version, and herdr and sops are fetched as release assets with a verified
# SHA-256 for the container's architecture — check.sh asserts every one of those
# pins. None is expressible as a package line, and more to the point all four
# are deliberately NON-fatal (`|| echo`), so that an npm outage or a GitHub
# hiccup costs the container a tool rather than costing it a create. Moving them
# into this fail-closed file would silently reverse that decision.
